full_judgment:
2. Plaintiff-respondent instituted Title Suit No. 106 of 1966 in theist Court of Subordinate Judge. Mymensingh, against the defendant-appellants praying for declaration of title to the land in suit appertaining to C.S. Plot No. 95 of Mouza Mymensingh town bearing Municipal holding No. 231 (present holding No. 66 and 66A) and for recovery of khas possession after demolishing the structures standing thereon. 

 4. Defendants 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement  denying the claim of the plaintiff. Their case was that the suit land was khas land of Maharaja Shashi Kinta Acharyya Chowdhury and appertained to the landlord’s khatian No. 95 of Mymensingh town. Then the Mymensingh Municipality had been entrusted by the Zaminder for protecting the land on behalf of the superior landlord and accordingly, the Municipality was nothing more than the custodian of the land belonging to the proprietor Zamindar. It was leased out to  Saileedra Nath Basu for 9 years and pucca structures were constructed with the knowledge and approval of the Municipality and the superior landlord and the defendants possessed the suit land openly and adversely. They further pleaded that after the acquisition of the rent receiving interests the said land vested in the Government and the defendants had become tenants directly under the Government and the Government had also recognised them. 

 "In- exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (1) of section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act No. XXVIII of 1951), as amended by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1956. (East Bengal Ordinance No. III of 1956) it is hereby notified, for the information of ail concerned that the Governor is pleased to acquire, with effect from the 14th April, 1256, all interests of all rent-receivers in their respective estates, taluks, tenures, holdings and tenancies situated in the district of '" ... including their interests in all sub-soil and rights to minerals in such estates taluks , tenures, holdings and tenancies except the interests and rights which have already been acquired by and have already vested in, the Provincial Government under the provisions of the said Act." For acquisition of khas lands. 

 "In exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (2) of section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act XXVIII of 1951) as amended by East Bengal Slate Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (East Bengal Ordinance III of 1956), it is hereby notified, for the information of all concerned that the Governor is pleased to acquire, with effect from the 14th April, 1956, all lands in the khas possession of all rent receivers situated in the district of .. other than the classes of lands coming under clauses (a) and (b) of sub-section (2) of section 20 and other than such lands as have already been acquired by, and nave already vested in, the Provincial Government under the provisions of the said Act". 

 11. When Mr. Pal was asked whether it was a estate of Maharaja or khas land he frankly conceded that the land in question would not answer the description either as the estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies or khas land. Since none of these descriptions of the land of the Municipality fit ill it does not come within the mischief of the law and the general notification. 

 13. It is undeniable fact that the land vested in the Municipality since 1932 and therefore, the defendant were only tenants of the land belonging to the Municipality by taking a temporary lease for nine years which however was renewed from time to time. The teamed Courts below unfortunately did not approach the facts of the case from the correct legal aspect. The High Court Division repelled the contention that after the wholesale acquisition by the Government the defendant has become a tenant under the Government and that the Maharaja has lost his paramount interest. This contention was repelled by the High Court Division by saying "the plaintiff is very much the owner of the suit land and cannot be denied any relief in the suit on the ground that it has lost its title," Mr. Pal argued that the question was not answered in the judgments of the courts below as to how this suit land vested in the Municipality and how it is exonerated from the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The answer is what we have given already that by the general notification affecting the rent receiving interest and the khas land of the rent receiver, the land which has vested with the Municipality since 1932 was not affected and therefore, the contentious of the defendants do not hold good, And. secondly the defendants' plea of adverse possession, as noticed already, has no substance. The trial court found that the defendants had constructed pucca structures in violation of the terms of the kabuliyat and these structures were raised some 20/25 years back. The view was taken that their possession "was adverse to the knowledge of Municipality' and in these circumstances "the Municipality was with the right of collecting cent and tax only as in the meantime the defendant 1 and his brother acquired tenancy right by adverse possession." The appellate court below though affirmed the judgment and order of the trial court took the view that the questions of adverse possession does not arise in this case and concluded that Sailendra continued to be a tenant by holding over.
